sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: 9:41 PM
case.hook: I put four sensors on the Palmetto Beach pier to watch a summer storm. (A sensor is a tool that measures something and records it.) At 9:41 PM, all four jumped at the same moment, and the pier lamp went dark.

strip.head: PIER DATA LOGGER · STATION 3
strip.sub: Friday night · one reading per minute
strip.alt: A strip chart with four lines from 9:35 to 9:47 PM. At 9:41 the light, sound and heat lines all spike, and the power line to the pier lamp drops to zero.
strip.note: Nobody was on the pier. Nobody touched the lamp post. So how did energy reach all four sensors at once? (Sam)

case.question: What happened on the pier at 9:41 PM, when nobody was there?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: You were the source three times. Each time, you knew energy moved because the receiver CHANGED: it warmed up, buzzed or squinted. A spike on a sensor is a receiver changing too.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: block the path
clues.t: Heat, light and sound crossed empty air with nothing touching. Electricity needed a path, and plastic in the wire stopped it.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: which way does heat go?
clues.t: Heat always moves from warmer to cooler. And lightning is a giant electric current that rushes from a cloud into whatever it hits.
Light arrives first and sound comes later. The shorter the gap, the closer the strike. At 9:41 the boom came only a split second after the flash.

solve.title: What happened at 9:41 PM?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Someone sneaked onto the pier and switched off the lamp.
options.why: Check the note and Clue 2. Nobody was there, and energy can cross the air without anyone touching anything.

options.t: Cold storm air moved into the lamp post and froze the lamp.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Cold doesn’t travel, heat does. And the heat line went UP.

options.t: Lightning struck the metal lamp post, right at the pier. Its electrical energy rushed down the post and burned out the lamp, and the bolt sent light, sound and heat through the air to every sensor.
options.why: Case cracked! The flash, the boom a split second later, the hot post and the dead lamp all point to a lightning strike right at the pier. Sam is putting up a lightning rod (a metal rod that gives lightning a safe path into the ground).

options.t: A big wave crashed over the sensors.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 4. Can a wave make a bright flash and a heat spike?

rateit.afterText: Today YOU are the energy source
rateit.title: Feel it, rate it
todo: Pick a move and really do it.
Slide the meter: how much did the receiver change?
Then pick where the energy went. Do all 3 moves.

why.t: The place the energy goes. You can’t see energy fly by, but you can feel or see the receiver change.

rateit.zeroLine: Nothing yet? Try it again a little longer, then slide the meter.

moves.do: Rub your palms together fast for 10 seconds. Then press them gently on your cheeks.
moves.rate: How much did your cheeks warm up?

recs.miss: What did you FEEL warm up?
Energy doesn’t disappear. Something got warmer. What was it?

moves.why: Rubbing made your palms warm. Then heat moved from your warm palms into your cooler cheeks.

moves.do: Put your fingertips gently on the front of your throat. Hum one long note.
moves.rate: How much buzz did your fingertips feel?
moves.recQ: Where did the sound energy go?

recs.t: Into my fingertips and my ears

recs.miss: Did your fingertips feel it? Could you hear it?
Sound is shaking. What shook, besides your throat?

moves.why: Your voice box shook (vibrated). The shaking traveled into your fingertips and through the air to your ears.

moves.do: Cover your eyes with your hands for 10 seconds. Then uncover them and look toward a window or a lamp. (Never look at the Sun.)
moves.rate: How bright did it seem when you uncovered your eyes?
moves.recQ: Where did the light energy go?

recs.miss: Your hands were in the way. What happened when you moved them?
It seemed bright! What part of you did the light reach?

moves.why: Light traveled across the room into your eyes. Your eyes changed: you squinted, and the dark centers of your eyes got smaller.

rateit.q: How did you know energy moved each time?

opts.t: Something at the other end changed. It warmed up, buzzed or squinted.
I saw the energy flying through the air.
opts.miss: You can’t see heat or sound flying by. What changed instead?
You felt it yourself! What changed in your cheeks, fingertips and eyes?

rateit.win: You were the source three times, and a receiver changed every time. Clue 1!

blockpath.title: Block the path
todo: Tap each gap. What is between the source and the receiver?
Drag a blocker into the gap (or tap a blocker, then the gap).
Watch the receiver. Did it stop changing?

why.t: If blocking the gap stops the change, then energy really was traveling through that gap.

blockpath.tapFirst: First tap the gap. What is in there, between the source and the receiver?
blockpath.trayLabel: Blockers (drag one into a gap, or tap it and then a gap)

scenes.gap: Only air! The fire never touches your hands, but they still get warm.
scenes.off: Your hands cool down. So the heat WAS crossing the air.

miss.umbrella: Never hold an umbrella near a fire! Try something solid and thick.
miss.earmuffs: Earmuffs block sound, not the heat from a fire.
miss.plastic: That little plastic piece fits inside a wire. Try something big and solid.

scenes.gap: Only air and empty space! The Sun is 93 million miles away, and its light still reaches the leaf.
scenes.on: The leaf is soaking up sunlight.
scenes.off: Shade! The light is blocked. So the light WAS crossing the air.

miss.earmuffs: Earmuffs go on ears, not leaves!
miss.plastic: That little plastic piece fits inside a wire. Try something big that makes shade.

scenes.gap: Only air! The drum is across the room, but the air carries its shaking to your ear.
scenes.on: Your eardrum is shaking with the beat.
scenes.off: Much quieter! So the sound WAS traveling through the air.

miss.board: A board helps a little, but sound bends around it. Try something right on your ears.
miss.umbrella: Sound goes right around an umbrella. What covers your ears?
miss.plastic: That little plastic piece fits inside a wire. What covers your ears?

scenes.gap: A wire! Here the energy needs a metal path. It can’t just cross the air.
scenes.off: Plastic doesn’t carry electricity, so the path is broken and the bulb goes dark.
scenes.missAny: The energy here travels inside the wire. Put something that blocks electricity INTO the wire.

blockpath.q: What did blocking the paths prove?

opts.t: Energy really was traveling across each gap, even through air with nothing touching.
Energy only moves when things touch.
opts.miss: Look at the gaps you tapped. Was anything touching the fire, the Sun or the drum?
Blockers stop energy. They don’t make it.

blockpath.win: Heat, light and sound crossed the air. Electricity needed its wire. Clue 2!

heatflow.afterText: four different WAYS energy can travel
heatflow.title: Which way does heat go?
todo: A glass of iced lemonade sits on a hot porch. Pick the arrow you think is true.
Press Wait one hour. Watch both thermometers.
Then drag the right way onto each Florida scene.

why.t: How warm something is. If its number goes up, energy moved in. If it goes down, energy moved out.

heatflow.alt: A model: a glass of iced lemonade on a sunny porch, a thermometer in the porch air and a thermometer in the lemonade.
heatflow.arrowQ: Which way does the energy go?

arrows.t: 🔥 Heat moves from the warm air INTO the lemonade
❄️ Cold moves from the lemonade OUT into the air

heatflow.rightAfter: Heat always moves from warmer to cooler. The warm porch air sent heat into the cold drink, so the ice melted. The air hardly changed because there is so much of it.
heatflow.wrongAfter: If cold were leaving the drink, the drink would get colder. But it got WARMER and the ice melted. Cold doesn’t travel. Pick the other arrow.
heatflow.cardsHead: Now name the way energy travels in each Florida scene

cards.why: Light traveled from the Sun. The sidewalk soaked it up and got hot enough to hurt bare feet.

miss.heat: The sidewalk does get hot in the end! But what traveled all the way from the Sun?

cards.why: The instruments shake the air. The shaking travels to your ears.
A giant electric current crashed through the air into the tree. It made light, sound and heat, too!

miss.light: You SEE the flash, but what rushed from the cloud INTO the tree?
miss.heat: The tree gets scorched, but what rushed from the cloud INTO the tree?

cards.why: The burner is hotter than the pan, so heat moves into the pan and then into the eggs.

miss.elec: Electricity runs the burner. But between the hot burner and the pan, what moves from warmer to cooler?

heatflow.q: Ice makes your drink cold. What is really happening?

opts.t: Heat moves from the warm drink into the colder ice.
Cold moves out of the ice into the drink.
opts.miss: Remember the lemonade. Which way does energy travel: warmer to cooler, or cooler to warmer?
The ice melts! Something moved into it.

heatflow.win: Heat moves from warmer to cooler, every time. And you named all four ways energy travels. Clue 3!

stormwatch.afterText: When you see a flash, start counting
stormwatch.title: Storm watch
todo: Press Start watching and keep your eyes on the sky.
Tap I SAW the flash as soon as it flashes.
Tap I HEARD the thunder when the boom comes. Turn your sound on!

why.t: Lightning heats the air so fast that the air bursts outward with a BOOM. The flash and the boom start at the same moment.

strikes.alt: Lightning bolts branch across a stormy night sky over Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
Lightning bolts hit the ocean and a tall metal mast at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
A lightning bolt hits the top of a tall metal mast at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
strikes.far: less than half a mile away. Get inside!

stormwatch.readyLine: Press Start watching, then keep your eyes on the sky.
stormwatch.countLine: Counting… now listen for the boom!
stormwatch.earlyLine: No flash yet! Wait until the sky lights up.
stormwatch.lateLine: Not yet! Listen. Tap when you HEAR the boom.
stormwatch.logLabel: Your storm log (every 5 seconds = about 1 mile)
stormwatch.safety: If you can hear thunder, lightning is close enough to strike you. Go inside a building or a hard-topped car, and wait 30 minutes after the last boom.
stormwatch.credit: Lightning at Kennedy Space Center, Florida: “Lightning Above the STS-8 Launch Pad” (NASA, 1983), “Lightning Strikes at Pad 39B” (NASA, May 2011) and “Lightning Strikes at Pad 39B” (NASA, August 2019). All public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
stormwatch.q: Why did you SEE each flash before you HEARD the thunder?

opts.t: Light travels almost a million times faster than sound.

opts.miss: The flash and the boom happen at the same moment. Which one travels faster?

opts.t: My ears are slower than my eyes.
opts.miss: Your ears work fast! The sound itself was slow getting to you.

stormwatch.win: Flash first, boom later. The shorter the gap, the closer the strike. Clue 4!

bulletin.station: Ray, the pier night guard · 9:41 PM
lines: Base, this is Ray at the pier gate. It’s 9:41.
I saw a [[light|huge white flash]] at the end of the pier, and right away a [[sound|BOOM so loud I felt it in my chest]].
Now the [[power|pier lamp is dark]], and there’s a [[heat|burnt smell by the metal post]].
[[x:Good to know for the case! But this isn’t a sign that energy arrived. Look for something that changed.|Nobody is out there]]. I’m staying inside the gate house. Over.
bulletin.win: Four ways energy arrived, all at 9:41. Ray stayed inside. Smart!

tool.name: Circuit tester
tool.teaser: Test a spoon, a key, a pencil and more. Which ones let electricity through?
tool.done: You tested every object. A circuit tester sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.q: What does a circuit tester do?
why.t: It has a small battery and a bulb. Touch both tips to something. If electricity can flow through it, the path is complete and the bulb lights.

circuittester.title: Conductor or insulator?
todo: Drag a thing onto the tester (or tap it).
Test all 7. (A real tester uses a small battery. Never test a wall outlet.)
circuittester.dropHere: Drop a thing on the tester

objects.note: Steel is a metal. Metals let electricity flow.
Keys are made of metal, like brass.
Coins are made of metals like copper and nickel.
Pencil “lead” is really graphite, a kind of carbon. It lets some electricity through, so the bulb glows.
Rubber blocks electricity. That’s why tool handles and boots for electricians use it.
Plastic blocks electricity, like the coating on a power cord.

q.q: Sam is putting a lightning rod on the pier. What should it be made of?

opts.t: Metal, like copper. It’s a great conductor.
opts.why: Right! A copper or aluminum rod gives lightning an easy path down a cable into the ground, away from the lamp and the people.
Plastic is an insulator. Lightning needs a path it can travel through.
Wood is an insulator, and it can catch fire. Which things lit your bulb?

q1.A: Energy can’t be made from nothing. What did it do in Block the path?
q1.B: Energy can’t be destroyed. Where did it go in the Warm-Up?

q2.B: A shout doesn’t warm your ear much. What did your fingertips feel when you hummed?
q2.C: There’s no wire between you and your friend. What travels through the air as shaking?

q3.A: The bulb is where the energy ends up. That makes it the receiver.
q3.C: The button opens and closes the path. Where does the energy come FROM?

welcome.label: Welcome · 9:41 PM
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Sam. Something strange happened on the Palmetto Beach pier last night. At 9:41, all four of my sensors jumped at once, and the pier lamp went dark. But nobody was there! Look at my strip chart. Find the red line. What could reach every sensor at the same moment?

warmup.label: Warm-Up · feel it, rate it (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Today, you are the energy source! Read the first card and really do it. Rub your hands, hum, and look at a light. After each one, slide the meter to show how much changed. Then pick where the energy went.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Rub your hands for “heat”; hum for “sound”; flick a flashlight for “light”.

part1.label: Part 1 · block the path (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here are four energy paths. Tap each gap first. What’s in there? Then drag a blocker into the gap, like the umbrella or the earmuffs. Watch the receiver. Did it stop changing?

part2.label: Part 2 · which way does heat go? (Clue 3)
part2.script: Iced lemonade on a hot porch! Pick an arrow. Does heat move in, or does cold move out? Press Wait one hour, and watch both thermometers. Then drag the right way onto each Florida scene.

explore.label: Part 4 · storm watch (Clue 4)
explore.script: A storm is rolling in. Turn your sound on and press Start watching. When the sky flashes, tap I saw the flash. When you hear the boom, tap I heard the thunder. Your storm log turns the seconds into miles.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab. Then answer two questions, fill in your energy hunt, and finish your C-E-R.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says energy only moves when things touch. Hmm. Think about the gaps you blocked and the thunder you counted. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! Lightning hit the pier lamp, and its energy reached every sensor through the air. Now I’m adding a lightning rod. Next time, you set up your own energy stations and collect evidence.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how energy moves, and how we know it moved?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Energy moves from a source to a receiver, even through the air.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “energy moves”, “source”, “receiver” and “through the air”. Those words hold the big idea. Small words like “a” and “the” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
